claim: A subset of neurons in the medial preoptic area (MPOA) that express galanin play crucial roles in regulating parental behavior in both sexes in mice.
source: Recent studies in mice demonstrate that a subset of neurons in the medial preoptic area (MPOA) that express galanin play crucial roles in regulating parental behavior in both sexes.
evidence: Cited from recent studies in mice without specific data presented in this manuscript

claim: A subset of MPOA galanin neurons occurred nearly exclusively in males in medaka.
source: Here, we report that, in medaka, a subset of MPOA galanin neurons occurred nearly exclusively in males, resulting from testicular androgen stimulation.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing male-biased expression in pPMp

claim: The male-biased MPOA galanin neurons in medaka result from testicular androgen stimulation.
source: Here, we report that, in medaka, a subset of MPOA galanin neurons occurred nearly exclusively in males, resulting from testicular androgen stimulation.
evidence: Supported by castration and androgen treatment experiments

claim: Galanin-deficient medaka showed a greatly reduced incidence of male–male aggressive chases.
source: Galanin-deficient medaka showed a greatly reduced incidence of male–male aggressive chases.
evidence: Demonstrated through behavioral tests of gal knockout lines

claim: Treatment of female medaka with androgen induced male-typical aggressive acts.
source: Furthermore, while treatment of female medaka with androgen induced male-typical aggressive acts, galanin deficiency in these females attenuated the effect of androgen on chases.
evidence: Shown through androgen treatment experiments on females

claim: Galanin deficiency in androgen-treated females attenuated the effect of androgen on chases.
source: Furthermore, while treatment of female medaka with androgen induced male-typical aggressive acts, galanin deficiency in these females attenuated the effect of androgen on chases.
evidence: Demonstrated through behavioral tests of androgen-treated gal knockout females

claim: The subset of MPOA galanin neurons most likely mediate androgen-dependent male–male chases given their male-biased and androgen-dependent nature.
source: Given their male-biased and androgen-dependent nature, the subset of MPOA galanin neurons most likely mediate androgen-dependent male–male chases.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of sexual dimorphism, androgen dependence, and behavioral phenotype

claim: Variability in the projection targets of the MPOA galanin neurons may account for the species-dependent functional differences in these evolutionarily conserved neural substrates.
source: Histological studies further suggested that variability in the projection targets of the MPOA galanin neurons may account for the species-dependent functional differences in these evolutionarily conserved neural substrates.
evidence: Based on histological comparison of projection patterns between medaka and mice

claim: A group of reciprocally connected brain regions that regulates social behaviors in concert with sex steroids and neuropeptides has been highly conserved over the 450 million years of vertebrate evolution.
source: A group of reciprocally connected brain regions that regulates social behaviors in concert with sex steroids and neuropeptides, sometimes referred to as the 'social behavior network', has been highly conserved over the 450 million years of vertebrate evolution (Newman, 1999; Goodson, 2005; O'Connell and Hofmann, 2012).
evidence: Cited from established literature on the social behavior network

claim: The preoptic area (POA) is the most highly conserved node of the social behavior network.
source: The preoptic area (POA) is the most highly conserved node of this network, containing subsets of steroid receptor- and neuropeptide-expressing neurons that regulate a wide range of social behaviors (O'Connell and Hofmann, 2012).
evidence: Cited from established literature

claim: A subset of neurons in the medial POA (MPOA) that express galanin play a crucial role in regulating parental behavior in both sexes in mice.
source: Recent evidence in mice demonstrates that a subset of neurons in the medial POA (MPOA) that express the pleiotropic neuropeptide galanin (abbreviated as GAL or Gal depending on species) play a crucial role in regulating parental behavior in both sexes (Wu et al., 2014; Kohl et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from recent mouse studies

claim: GAL-expressing neurons are commonly found in the MPOA of vertebrates, including teleost fish.
source: GAL-expressing neurons are commonly found in the MPOA of vertebrates, including teleost fish, the majority of which do not provide parental care (Fischer and O'Connell, 2017).
evidence: Cited from comparative literature

claim: The majority of teleost fish do not provide parental care.
source: GAL-expressing neurons are commonly found in the MPOA of vertebrates, including teleost fish, the majority of which do not provide parental care (Fischer and O'Connell, 2017).
evidence: Cited from literature on teleost behavior

claim: Males have many more MPOA Gal neurons than females in several teleost species.
source: Curiously, studies in several teleost species have consistently shown that males have many more MPOA Gal neurons than females (Cornbrooks and Parsons, 1991; Rao et al., 1996; Rodríguez et al., 2003; Tripp and Bass, 2020).
evidence: Cited from multiple teleost studies

claim: In mammals, either there is no sex difference in the number of MPOA GAL neurons, or the direction of the sex difference (if any) varies among species and even within strains in mice.
source: This contrasts with the situation in mammals, where either there is no sex difference in the number of these neurons, or the direction of the sex difference (if any) varies among species and even within strains in mice (Bloch et al., 1993; Park et al., 1997; Mathieson et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from mammalian literature

claim: Gal neurons in the teleost MPOA are assumed to be involved in some male-biased behavior.
source: Based on this distinctive feature, Gal neurons in the teleost MPOA are assumed to be involved in some male-biased behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the male-biased expression pattern

claim: MPOA Gal neurons are activated during mating in midshipman fish, suggesting they have a role in mating behavior.
source: Indeed, studies in midshipman fish (Porichthys notatus) have shown that MPOA Gal neurons are activated during mating, thereby suggesting that they have a role in mating behavior (Tripp and Bass, 2020; Tripp et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from midshipman fish studies

claim: No attempt has been made to directly test the behavioral role of MPOA Gal neurons in teleosts prior to this study.
source: To our knowledge, however, no attempt has been made to directly test these ideas.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field

claim: The mechanism that causes the male-biased sex difference in teleost Gal neurons remains to be elucidated.
source: Furthermore, the mechanism that causes the male-biased sex difference in teleost Gal neurons remains to be elucidated.
evidence: Statement about gaps in knowledge

claim: In medaka, females spawn once daily over the spawning period, whereas males can spawn multiple times a day.
source: In medaka, females spawn once daily over the spawning period, whereas males can spawn multiple times a day (Weir and Grant, 2010).
evidence: Cited from medaka behavioral literature

claim: Neither male nor female medaka provide parental care after spawning.
source: Neither males nor females provide parental care after spawning.
evidence: Statement about medaka behavior

claim: Adult male medaka compete aggressively for territories and access to food and mates, whereas females engage in far less aggression.
source: Adult males compete aggressively for territories and access to food and mates, whereas females engage in far less aggression (Grant and Foam, 2002).
evidence: Cited from medaka behavioral literature

claim: The medaka protein identified represents the medaka ortholog of GAL.
source: Phylogenetic tree analysis confirmed that this protein represented the medaka ortholog of GAL (Figure 1A).
evidence: Confirmed by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: A 0.8 kb gal transcript was much more abundant in the adult male brain than in the female brain.
source: Northern blot analysis revealed the presence of a 0.8 kb gal transcript, which was much more abundant in the adult male brain than in the female brain (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown by Northern blot in Figure 1B

claim: There is a male-biased sexual dimorphism in gal expression in the adult medaka brain.
source: This result was confirmed by quantitative real-time PCR analysis, which showed a male-biased sexual dimorphism in gal expression in the adult brain (p<0.0001, t = 19.3, df = 7.12; unpaired t-test with Welch's correction) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Confirmed by real-time PCR with statistical significance shown in Figure 1C

claim: Neurons expressing gal were observed in the aPMp/PPa, pPMp, and PPp in the MPOA, and the NAT/NVT/NRL in the hypothalamus of the adult brain of both sexes.
source: Neurons expressing gal were observed in the anterior part of the parvocellular portion of the magnocellular preoptic nucleus (aPMp)/anterior parvocellular preoptic nucleus (PPa), the posterior part of the parvocellular portion of the magnocellular preoptic nucleus (pPMp), and the posterior parvocellular preoptic nucleus (PPp) in the MPOA, and the anterior tuberal nucleus (NAT)/ventral tuberal nucleus (NVT)/lateral recess nucleus (NRL) in the hypothalamus of the adult brain of both sexes (Figure 1D–G; abbreviations for medaka brain nuclei are given in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Shown by in situ hybridization in Figures 1D-G

claim: Striking sexual dimorphism was observed in pPMp, where gal-expressing neurons occurred much more abundantly in males than in females.
source: Although there were no sex differences in these spatial patterns, striking sexual dimorphism was observed in pPMp, where gal-expressing neurons occurred much more abundantly in males than in females (p<0.0001, t = 12.1, df = 8; unpaired t-test) (Figure 1D and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization with statistical analysis shown in Figures 1D and G

claim: NAT/NVT/NRL contained a slightly higher, but comparable, number of gal-expressing neurons in males than in females.
source: In addition to pPMp, NAT/NVT/NRL contained a slightly higher, but comparable, number of gal-expressing neurons in males than in females (p=0.047, t = 2.35, df = 8; unpaired t-test) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown by quantification in Figure 1D with statistical analysis

claim: pPMp in the MPOA is the major source of the sexual dimorphism in overall gal expression in the medaka brain.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that pPMp in the MPOA is the major source of the sexual dimorphism in overall gal expression in the medaka brain.
evidence: Concluded from the in situ hybridization data

claim: The male bias in gal expression increased steadily with age.
source: Examination of brains at different ages by real-time PCR revealed that the male bias in gal expression increased steadily with age (main effect of sex: F (1, 56)=464, p<0.0001; main effect of age: F (3, 56)=180, p<0.0001; and interaction between sex and age: F (3, 56)=106, p<0.0001) (Figure 1H).
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR analysis across developmental stages in Figure 1H

claim: gal was expressed at significantly higher levels in male than in female brains as early as 2 months of age.
source: gal was expressed at significantly higher levels in male than in female brains as early as 2 months of age (p=0.0002, t = 4.39, df = 56; Bonferroni's post hoc test), when secondary sexual characteristics were well-developed but spawning had not yet occurred (spawning started at 3 months).
evidence: Demonstrated by real-time PCR with statistical analysis

claim: No significant sex difference in brain gal expression was observed at 1 month of age, when secondary sexual characteristics began to appear.
source: No significant sex difference in brain gal expression was observed at an earlier age (1 month), when secondary sexual characteristics began to appear.
evidence: Shown by real-time PCR analysis

claim: Sex-reversed XX males exhibited the same high level of brain gal expression as typical XY males.
source: Real-time PCR analysis revealed that sex-reversed XX males exhibited the same high level of brain gal expression as typical XY males, whereas sex-reversed XY females showed a much lower level (p<0.0001, t = 17.2, df = 28 versus XY males; p<0.0001, t = 15.8, df = 28 versus XX males; Bonferroni's post hoc test), comparable to that in typical XX females (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by real-time PCR analysis of sex-reversed fish shown in Figure 2A

claim: Sex-reversed XY females showed a much lower level of brain gal expression, comparable to that in typical XX females.
source: Real-time PCR analysis revealed that sex-reversed XX males exhibited the same high level of brain gal expression as typical XY males, whereas sex-reversed XY females showed a much lower level (p<0.0001, t = 17.2, df = 28 versus XY males; p<0.0001, t = 15.8, df = 28 versus XX males; Bonferroni's post hoc test), comparable to that in typical XX females (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by real-time PCR analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: The number of gal-expressing neurons in each brain nucleus of sex-reversed XX males and XY females was roughly equivalent to that in typical XY males and XX females, respectively.
source: Consistent with these results, in situ hybridization analysis showed that the number of gal-expressing neurons in each brain nucleus of sex-reversed XX males and XY females was roughly equivalent to that in typical XY males and XX females, respectively.
evidence: Shown by in situ hybridization analysis

claim: XX males had many more gal-expressing neurons in pPMp as compared with XY females.
source: XX males had many more gal-expressing neurons in pPMp (p<0.0001, t = 8.71, df = 8; unpaired t-test) and slightly more gal-expressing neurons in NAT/NVT/NRL (p=0.048, t = 2.33, df = 8; unpaired t-test) as compared with XY females (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization with statistical analysis shown in Figures 2B and C

claim: The pattern of brain gal expression is independent of sex chromosome complement but linked to gonadal phenotype.
source: These results indicate that the pattern of brain gal expression is independent of sex chromosome complement but linked to gonadal phenotype.
evidence: Concluded from sex-reversal experiments

claim: The level of brain gal expression in males was significantly reduced by castration.
source: In males, the level of brain gal expression, as measured by real-time PCR, was significantly reduced by castration (p=0.016, t = 3.04, df = 27; Bonferroni's post hoc test), and restored by treatment with KT (p<0.0001, t = 6.74, df = 27; Bonferroni's post hoc test) but not E2 (p>0.99, t = 0.679, df = 27; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by real-time PCR analysis of castrated males shown in Figure 2D

claim: Brain gal expression in castrated males was restored by treatment with KT but not E2.
source: In males, the level of brain gal expression, as measured by real-time PCR, was significantly reduced by castration (p=0.016, t = 3.04, df = 27; Bonferroni's post hoc test), and restored by treatment with KT (p<0.0001, t = 6.74, df = 27; Bonferroni's post hoc test) but not E2 (p>0.99, t = 0.679, df = 27; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by real-time PCR analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Castration caused a significant reduction in the number of gal-expressing neurons in pPMp, which was restored by KT treatment but not by E2 treatment.
source: In accordance with these results, in situ hybridization revealed that castration caused a significant reduction in the number of gal-expressing neurons in pPMp (p=0.0048, t = 3.79, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test), which was restored by KT treatment (p=0.0052, t = 3.75, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) but not by E2 treatment (p=0.28, t = 1.79, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2E and F), although E2 treatment increased the number of gal-expressing neurons in aPMp/pPPa (p=0.013, t = 3.33, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown by in situ hybridization analysis in Figures 2E and F

claim: E2 treatment increased the number of gal-expressing neurons in aPMp/pPPa in castrated males.
source: In accordance with these results, in situ hybridization revealed that castration caused a significant reduction in the number of gal-expressing neurons in pPMp (p=0.0048, t = 3.79, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test), which was restored by KT treatment (p=0.0052, t = 3.75, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) but not by E2 treatment (p=0.28, t = 1.79, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2E and F), although E2 treatment increased the number of gal-expressing neurons in aPMp/pPPa (p=0.013, t = 3.33, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown by in situ hybridization in Figure 2E

claim: Ovariectomy caused a significant increase in the number of gal-expressing neurons in pPMp in females.
source: However, in situ hybridization revealed that ovariectomy caused a significant increase in the number of gal-expressing neurons in pPMp (p=0.020, t = 3.11, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test), which was further enhanced by subsequent KT treatment (p=0.0008, t = 4.63, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figures 2H and I

claim: The increase in gal-expressing neurons in pPMp after ovariectomy was further enhanced by subsequent KT treatment.
source: However, in situ hybridization revealed that ovariectomy caused a significant increase in the number of gal-expressing neurons in pPMp (p=0.020, t = 3.11, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test), which was further enhanced by subsequent KT treatment (p=0.0008, t = 4.63, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: Shown by in situ hybridization in Figures 2H and I

claim: The increase in gal-expressing neurons in pPMp after ovariectomy was significantly attenuated by E2 treatment.
source: Conversely, the increase was significantly attenuated by E2 treatment (p=0.040, t = 2.79, df = 16; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figures 2H and I

claim: High circulating levels of androgen derived from the testis cause a marked increase in gal-expressing neurons in pPMp in adult males.
source: Together, these results indicate that high circulating levels of androgen derived from the testis cause a marked increase in gal-expressing neurons in pPMp in adult males, whereas the absence of androgen stimulation in adult females means that these neurons remain at basal levels.
evidence: Concluded from gonadectomy and hormone treatment experiments

claim: The absence of androgen stimulation in adult females means that gal-expressing neurons in pPMp remain at basal levels.
source: Together, these results indicate that high circulating levels of androgen derived from the testis cause a marked increase in gal-expressing neurons in pPMp in adult males, whereas the absence of androgen stimulation in adult females means that these neurons remain at basal levels.
evidence: Concluded from gonadectomy and hormone treatment experiments

claim: gal-expressing neurons in pPMp are diminished in adult males deprived of androgen.
source: In addition, these neurons are diminished in adult males deprived of androgen and, conversely, are induced in adult females deprived of estrogen and supplemented with androgen.
evidence: Demonstrated by castration experiments

claim: gal-expressing neurons in pPMp are induced in adult females deprived of estrogen and supplemented with androgen.
source: In addition, these neurons are diminished in adult males deprived of androgen and, conversely, are induced in adult females deprived of estrogen and supplemented with androgen.
evidence: Demonstrated by ovariectomy and hormone treatment experiments

claim: ara was expressed in a large proportion of gal-expressing neurons in males and in some of the sparse gal-expressing neurons in females.
source: ara was expressed in a large proportion of gal-expressing neurons in males and in some of the sparse gal-expressing neurons in females, whereas none of these neurons were positive for arb expression in either sex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by double in situ hybridization in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: None of the gal-expressing neurons in pPMp were positive for arb expression in either sex.
source: ara was expressed in a large proportion of gal-expressing neurons in males and in some of the sparse gal-expressing neurons in females, whereas none of these neurons were positive for arb expression in either sex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by double in situ hybridization in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: esr1 was expressed in a large proportion of gal-expressing neurons in both sexes.
source: esr1 was expressed in a large proportion of gal-expressing neurons in both sexes, whereas esr2a and esr2b were expressed in these neurons only in males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by double in situ hybridization in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: esr2a and esr2b were expressed in gal-expressing neurons only in males.
source: esr1 was expressed in a large proportion of gal-expressing neurons in both sexes, whereas esr2a and esr2b were expressed in these neurons only in males (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by double in situ hybridization in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The stimulatory action of androgen on gal-expressing neurons in pPMp is mediated via ara.
source: These results suggest that androgen and estrogen may directly act on gal-expressing neurons in pPMp and that, if so, the stimulatory action of androgen is mediated via ara, while the inhibitory action of estrogen seen in females is mediated via esr1.
evidence: Inferred from receptor expression patterns

claim: The inhibitory action of estrogen on gal-expressing neurons in pPMp in females is mediated via esr1.
source: These results suggest that androgen and estrogen may directly act on gal-expressing neurons in pPMp and that, if so, the stimulatory action of androgen is mediated via ara, while the inhibitory action of estrogen seen in females is mediated via esr1.
evidence: Inferred from receptor expression patterns

claim: Successful ablation of gal was confirmed by the complete loss of Gal immunoreactivity in homozygous knockout brains from both lines.
source: Successful ablation of gal was confirmed by the complete loss of Gal immunoreactivity in homozygous knockout brains from both lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1); the specificity of the anti-GAL antibody used was verified by simultaneous application of immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization, which showed that the antibody selectively labeled neuronal cell bodies expressing the gal transcript (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Most heterozygous and homozygous knockout males from the Δ2 and Δ10 lines spawned successfully, similar to wild-type males.
source: The mating behavior tests revealed that most heterozygous and homozygous knockout males from the Δ2 and Δ10 lines spawned successfully, similar to wild-type males.
evidence: Shown by mating behavior tests

claim: There were no significant differences in any of the detailed parameters of mating behavior among wild-type, heterozygous knockout, and homozygous knockout males of either line.
source: Moreover, there were no significant differences in any of the detailed parameters of mating behavior among wild-type, heterozygous knockout, and homozygous knockout males of either line (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by mating behavior analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Females did not show significant differences in any of the parameters of mating behavior among genotypes.
source: Similarly, females did not show significant differences in any of the parameters of mating behavior among genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by mating behavior analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous knockout males from the Δ2 and Δ10 lines exhibited significantly fewer chases as compared with wild-type males.
source: The aggressive behavior tests revealed that heterozygous and homozygous knockout males from the Δ2 and Δ10 lines exhibited significantly fewer chases as compared with wild-type males (p=0.0003, t = 5.31, df = 14 for +/Δ2; p=0.0020, t = 4.36, df = 14 for Δ2/Δ2; p=0.0087, t = 3.55, df = 15 for +/Δ10; and p=0.012, t = 3.40, df = 15 for Δ10/Δ10; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by aggressive behavior tests shown in Figures 3A and B

claim: Homozygous knockout males from the Δ2 line performed fewer chases as compared with wild-type males in all time intervals, with significant differences in the first 10 min.
source: Examination of the number of chases in each 5 min interval during the 20-min test period revealed that homozygous knockout males performed fewer chases as compared with wild-type males in all time intervals, with significant differences in the first 10 min for the Δ2 line (main effect of genotype: F (1, 10)=27.2, p=0.0004; main effect of time: F (3, 30)=1.05, p=0.38; interaction between genotype and time: F (3, 30)=2.29, p=0.098; p=0.0004, t = 4.31, df = 40 at 0–5 min; p=0.017, t = 3.03, df = 40 at 5–10 min; p=0.73, t = 1.36, df = 40 at 10–15 min; and p>0.99, t = 0.957, df = 40 at 15–20 min; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 3C) and in the last 10 min for the Δ10 line (main effect of genotype: F (1, 10)=12.3, p=0.0057; main effect of time: F (3, 30)=8.62, p=0.0003; interaction between genotype and time: F (3, 30)=3.07, p=0.043; p>0.99, t = 0.519, df = 40 at 0–5 min; p=0.28, t = 1.87, df = 40 at 5–10 min; p=0.0013, t = 3.94, df = 40 at 10–15 min; and p=0.014, t = 3.11, df = 40 at 15–20 min; Bonferroni's post hoc test) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown by time-course analysis in Figures 3C and D

claim: Many males both initiated and received chases regardless of their genotype.
source: Further analysis of the number of chases initiated and received by each individual male revealed that not a few but rather many males both initiated and received chases regardless of their genotype (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Shown by individual analysis in Figures 3E and F

claim: The +/Δ2 and Δ2/Δ2 males showed significantly fewer fin displays relative to wild-type males.
source: The +/Δ2 and Δ2/Δ2 males also showed significantly fewer fin displays relative to wild-type males (p=0.0028, t = 4.18, df = 14 for +/Δ2; p=0.0067, t = 3.73, df = 14 for Δ2/Δ2; Bonferroni's post hoc test); however, no similar trend was observed for Δ10 males, thus, there was a lack of reproducibility between the lines (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Shown by aggressive behavior tests in Figures 3A and B

claim: There were no significant differences in the number of circles, strikes, or bites among males of any genotype.
source: There were no significant differences in the number of circles, strikes, or bites among males of any genotype (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Shown by aggressive behavior tests in Figures 3A and B

claim: Females of all genotypes including wild-type exhibited no or very few aggressive acts.
source: In contrast to males, females of all genotypes including wild-type exhibited no or very few aggressive acts, and there were no significant differences in any of the acts evaluated among them (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Shown by aggressive behavior tests in Figures 3G and H

claim: Genetic ablation of gal in medaka resulted in a specific behavioral deficit in male–male chases.
source: In summary, genetic ablation of gal in medaka resulted in a specific behavioral deficit in male–male chases, indicating that gal plays a role exclusively in this aggressive behavioral act.
evidence: Concluded from knockout behavioral experiments

claim: gal plays a role exclusively in male-male chases.
source: In summary, genetic ablation of gal in medaka resulted in a specific behavioral deficit in male–male chases, indicating that gal plays a role exclusively in this aggressive behavioral act.
evidence: Concluded from the specific behavioral deficit observed

claim: Female medaka display male-typical aggressive behaviors, including chases, when treated with androgen as adults.
source: Our preliminary data indicated that female medaka display male-typical aggressive behaviors, including chases, when treated with androgen as adults.
evidence: Stated as preliminary observation

claim: Androgen treatment significantly increased the number of chases, fin displays, and bites in the two gal knockout lines.
source: Androgen treatment significantly increased the number of chases, fin displays, and bites in the two lines (main effect of androgen treatment: F (1, 20)=33.7, p<0.0001 and F (1, 20)=177, p<0.0001 for chases in Δ2 and Δ10, respectively; F (1, 20)=3.62, p=0.072 and F (1, 20)=14.4, p=0.0011 for fin displays in Δ2 and Δ10, respectively; and F (1, 20)=26.6, p<0.0001 and F (1, 20)=313, p<0.0001 for bites in Δ2 and Δ10, respectively) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by androgen treatment experiments shown in Figures 4A and B

claim: Homozygous knockout females performed significantly fewer chases relative to wild-type females after androgen treatment.
source: Although there were no significant between-genotype differences in fin displays or bites, the homozygous knockout females performed significantly fewer chases relative to wild-type females (main effect of genotype: F (1, 20)=10.2, p=0.0046 and F (1, 20)=36.9, p<0.0001 in Δ2 and Δ10, respectively; interaction between androgen treatment and genotype: F (1, 20)=11.5, p=0.0029 and F (1, 20)=36.9, p<0.0001 in Δ2 and Δ10, respectively; and Bonferroni's post hoc test: p=0.0003, t = 4.65, df = 20 and p<0.0001, t = 8.60, df = 20 in Δ2 and Δ10, respectively) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Shown by androgen treatment experiments in Figures 4A and B

claim: Gal-immunoreactive neurons were apparent in pPMp of wild-type females after androgen treatment, but not homozygous knockout females.
source: As expected, Gal-immunoreactive neurons were apparent in pPMp of wild-type females, but not homozygous knockout females (Figure 4C).
evidence: Shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 4C

claim: Androgen induces male-typical aggressive behaviors in females, but genetic ablation of gal specifically attenuates the effect of androgen on chases.
source: These results demonstrate that androgen induces male-typical aggressive behaviors in females, but genetic ablation of gal specifically attenuates the effect of androgen on chases.
evidence: Concluded from androgen treatment experiments in knockout females

claim: Dense plexuses of Gal-immunoreactive axons were observed in the ventrorostral part of the telencephalon, MPOA, hypothalamus, and pituitary of both sexes.
source: Dense plexuses of Gal-immunoreactive axons were observed in the ventrorostral part of the telencephalon, MPOA, hypothalamus, and pituitary of both sexes (Figure 5), suggesting that these axons arise from gal-expressing neurons in aPMp/PPa, PPp, and NAT/NVT/NRL, which occur in both sexes.
evidence: Shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 5

claim: In males, additional Gal-immunoreactive axons were found in many areas of the brain, with particular abundance in the dorsocaudal part of the telencephalon, thalamus, midbrain, cerebellum, and medulla oblongata.
source: In males, additional Gal-immunoreactive axons were found in many areas of the brain, with particular abundance in the dorsocaudal part of the telencephalon, thalamus, midbrain (optic tectum and tegmentum), cerebellum, and medulla oblongata (Figure 5).
evidence: Shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 5

claim: The additional Gal-immunoreactive axons observed in males originate from the male-dominant sexually dimorphic gal-expressing neurons in pPMp.
source: These additional axons were not observed in females, suggesting that they originate from the male-dominant sexually dimorphic gal-expressing neurons in pPMp.
evidence: Inferred from the male-specific distribution pattern

claim: Activation of Galr1 caused a 9.8-fold reduction in intracellular cAMP levels, with an EC50 of 21 pM.
source: Activation of Galr1 caused a 9.8-fold reduction in intracellular cAMP levels, with a Gal concentration for half-maximal effect (EC50) of 21 pM.
evidence: Demonstrated by receptor activation assays

claim: Activation of Galr2 increased cAMP levels 3.3-fold with an EC50 value of 6.8 nM.
source: By contrast, activation of Galr2 increased cAMP levels 3.3-fold with a much higher EC50 value of 6.8 nM.
evidence: Demonstrated by receptor activation assays

claim: Activation of both Galr1 and Galr2 increased intracellular Ca2+ levels with fairly similar EC50 values (130 and 800 nM, respectively).
source: Activation of both Galr1 and Galr2 increased intracellular Ca2+ levels with fairly similar EC50 values (130 and 800 nM, respectively), but Galr2 activation evoked a much higher maximal level as compared with Galr1 activation (76-fold versus 3.3-fold).
evidence: Demonstrated by receptor activation assays

claim: Galr2 activation evoked a much higher maximal Ca2+ level as compared with Galr1 activation (76-fold versus 3.3-fold).
source: Activation of both Galr1 and Galr2 increased intracellular Ca2+ levels with fairly similar EC50 values (130 and 800 nM, respectively), but Galr2 activation evoked a much higher maximal level as compared with Galr1 activation (76-fold versus 3.3-fold).
evidence: Demonstrated by receptor activation assays

claim: Activation of both Galr1 and Galr2 moderately stimulated MAPK activity (respectively, 6.2- and 16-fold maximal stimulation; and 40 and 72 nM EC50).
source: Activation of both Galr1 and Galr2 also moderately stimulated mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activity (respectively, 6.2- and 16-fold maximal stimulation; and 40 and 72 nM EC50).
evidence: Demonstrated by receptor activation assays

claim: In medaka, Gal signaling via Galr1 is primarily inhibitory, causing marked suppression of the cAMP pathway.
source: In medaka, therefore, Gal signaling via Galr1 is primarily inhibitory, causing marked suppression of the cAMP pathway, whereas that via Galr2 is excitatory, mediated mainly through a robust stimulation of Ca2+ flux.
evidence: Concluded from receptor activation assays

claim: Gal signaling via Galr2 is excitatory, mediated mainly through a robust stimulation of Ca2+ flux.
source: In medaka, therefore, Gal signaling via Galr1 is primarily inhibitory, causing marked suppression of the cAMP pathway, whereas that via Galr2 is excitatory, mediated mainly through a robust stimulation of Ca2+ flux.
evidence: Concluded from receptor activation assays

claim: GALR1 and GALR2 are primarily coupled to inhibitory Gi/Go and excitatory Gq/G11 proteins, respectively, in mammals.
source: These findings are consistent with studies in mammals showing that GALR1 and GALR2 are primarily coupled to inhibitory Gi/Go and excitatory Gq/G11 proteins, respectively (Lang et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from mammalian literature

claim: There were no apparent sex differences in the spatial expression patterns of galr1 or galr2.
source: There were no apparent sex differences in the spatial expression patterns of either receptor.
evidence: Observed from in situ hybridization analysis

claim: Gal can have both inhibitory and excitatory effects in the medaka brain via the activation of, respectively, Galr1 and Galr2.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Gal can have both inhibitory and excitatory effects in the medaka brain via the activation of, respectively, Galr1 and Galr2, which are widely but differentially distributed throughout the brain.
evidence: Concluded from receptor characterization and expression analysis

claim: Galr1 and Galr2 are widely but differentially distributed throughout the medaka brain.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Gal can have both inhibitory and excitatory effects in the medaka brain via the activation of, respectively, Galr1 and Galr2, which are widely but differentially distributed throughout the brain.
evidence: Shown by in situ hybridization analysis

claim: The sexual dimorphism in pPMp Gal neurons is conserved in teleosts.
source: Although not specifying the exact neuronal population, studies in several other teleosts have also demonstrated a male-biased abundance of MPOA Gal neurons (Cornbrooks and Parsons, 1991; Rao et al., 1996; Rodríguez et al., 2003; Tripp and Bass, 2020), suggesting that the sexual dimorphism in pPMp Gal neurons is conserved in teleosts.
evidence: Inferred from comparative studies across teleost species

claim: Sex differences in MPOA GAL neurons are species-specific and even strain-specific in mice.
source: This differs substantially from the situation in mammals, where sex differences in MPOA GAL neurons are species-specific and even strain-specific in mice (Bloch et al., 1993; Park et al., 1997; Mathieson et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from mammalian literature

claim: In mammals, sex differences in MPOA GAL neurons are established during fetal life.
source: In mammals, sex differences in MPOA GAL neurons are established during fetal life; this process is mediated by testicular testosterone, largely through its aromatase-mediated conversion in the brain to E2, which subsequently binds to ER (Bloch et al., 1993; Park et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from mammalian developmental studies

claim: The sex difference in pPMp Gal neurons in medaka emerges at the onset of puberty.
source: By contrast, we found that the sex difference in pPMp Gal neurons in medaka emerges at the onset of puberty and is mediated by testicular KT (a non-aromatizable androgen), which acts directly via AR without conversion to E2.
evidence: Demonstrated by developmental and hormone manipulation experiments

claim: The sex difference in pPMp Gal neurons in medaka is mediated by testicular KT, which acts directly via AR without conversion to E2.
source: By contrast, we found that the sex difference in pPMp Gal neurons in medaka emerges at the onset of puberty and is mediated by testicular KT (a non-aromatizable androgen), which acts directly via AR without conversion to E2.
evidence: Demonstrated by hormone manipulation experiments

claim: The sex difference in pPMp Gal neurons in medaka is independent of sex chromosome complement.
source: In addition, examination of sex-reversed medaka revealed that this sex difference is independent of sex chromosome complement and, more importantly, treatment of adult females with KT induced a significant increase in pPMp Gal neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by sex-reversal experiments

claim: Treatment of adult female medaka with KT induced a significant increase in pPMp Gal neurons.
source: In addition, examination of sex-reversed medaka revealed that this sex difference is independent of sex chromosome complement and, more importantly, treatment of adult females with KT induced a significant increase in pPMp Gal neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by hormone treatment experiments

claim: Treating adult female rats and ferrets with testosterone/E2 did not increase GAL neurons or their axons in the MPOA.
source: This is in stark contrast to the findings in rats and ferrets, where treating adult females with testosterone/E2 did not increase GAL neurons or their axons in the MPOA (Park et al., 1997; Polston and Simerly, 2003).
evidence: Cited from mammalian studies

claim: The sex difference in MPOA Gal neurons in medaka depends largely or even perhaps solely on the pubertal/adult sex steroid milieu and can be reversed in adulthood.
source: Therefore, the sex difference in MPOA Gal neurons in medaka depends largely or even perhaps solely on the pubertal/adult sex steroid milieu and can be reversed in adulthood, whereas that in mammals is irrevocably established early in life and, as a result, is robust in adulthood.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of medaka and mammalian data

claim: The sex difference in MPOA GAL neurons in mammals is irrevocably established early in life and is robust in adulthood.
source: Therefore, the sex difference in MPOA Gal neurons in medaka depends largely or even perhaps solely on the pubertal/adult sex steroid milieu and can be reversed in adulthood, whereas that in mammals is irrevocably established early in life and, as a result, is robust in adulthood.
evidence: Cited from mammalian literature

claim: Different aggressive acts are regulated by separate, albeit interacting, neural circuits.
source: It seems likely that different aggressive acts are regulated by separate, albeit interacting, neural circuits and that MPOA Gal neurons may be specifically embedded within the circuit mediating chases, acting downstream of androgen/AR signaling, which seems to affect most, if not all, circuits.
evidence: Inferred from the specific behavioral deficit in chases

claim: MPOA Gal neurons may be specifically embedded within the circuit mediating chases, acting downstream of androgen/AR signaling.
source: It seems likely that different aggressive acts are regulated by separate, albeit interacting, neural circuits and that MPOA Gal neurons may be specifically embedded within the circuit mediating chases, acting downstream of androgen/AR signaling, which seems to affect most, if not all, circuits.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral and hormone manipulation data

claim: Sexually dimorphic social behaviors are regulated in a modular manner by multiple sexually dimorphic genes acting downstream of sex steroid signaling.
source: This assumption is compatible with the view that sexually dimorphic social behaviors are regulated in a modular manner by multiple sexually dimorphic genes acting downstream of sex steroid signaling (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from literature on behavioral regulation

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous males displayed similar defects in chases.
source: Our results also show that heterozygous and homozygous males displayed similar defects in chases.
evidence: Observed from behavioral tests

claim: The level of the Gal peptide conferred by a single allele may be insufficient for normal male–male chases.
source: Although we do not have additional data to clarify this finding, the level of the Gal peptide conferred by a single allele may be insufficient for normal male–male chases.
evidence: Speculated based on the haploinsufficiency phenotype

claim: Haploinsufficiency causing similar behavioral phenotypes in heterozygotes and homozygotes has been reported for several genes relevant to social interaction and communication.
source: Haploinsufficiency causing similar behavioral phenotypes in heterozygotes and homozygotes has been reported for several genes relevant to social interaction and communication, including Shank3 (encoding an excitatory synapse scaffolding protein) and Sh3rf2 (encoding a putative ubiquitin E3 ligase) (Bozdagi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from literature on behavioral genetics

claim: In mice, MPOA GAL neurons promote the motivation to engage in parenting in part by suppressing aggression.
source: It should be noted that, in mice, MPOA GAL neurons promote the motivation to engage in parenting in part by suppressing aggression (Wu et al., 2014; Kohl et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from mouse studies

claim: An evolutionarily conserved subset of neurons in the social behavior network can serve different, even opposite (affiliative versus agonistic), functions across species.
source: This is in marked contrast to our findings in medaka, where MPOA Gal neurons were found to promote aggression, suggesting that an evolutionarily conserved subset of neurons in the social behavior network can serve different, even opposite (affiliative versus agonistic), functions across species.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of medaka and mouse data

claim: Differences in the regional densities of vasopressin and oxytocin receptors underlie variation in pair bonding in closely related monogamous and non-monogamous vole species.
source: For example, differences in the regional densities of vasopressin and oxytocin receptors, particularly in the ventral pallidum and nucleus accumbens, respectively, underlie variation in pair bonding in closely related monogamous and non-monogamous vole species (Walum and Young, 2018).
evidence: Cited from vole studies

claim: Vasopressin and oxytocin receptor densities in the lateral septum correlate well with variation in the propensity of different finch species to flock.
source: Similarly, vasopressin and oxytocin receptor densities in the lateral septum correlate well with variation in the propensity of different finch species to flock (Kelly and Goodson, 2014).
evidence: Cited from finch studies

claim: The altered functional role of neuropeptides can underlie behavioral variation across species.
source: Our findings demonstrate that the altered functional role of neuropeptides can underlie the behavioral variation.
evidence: Concluded from the comparative analysis of medaka and mice

claim: The functional alteration of neuropeptides may result from differences in the sites of action of neuropeptides.
source: Of note, this functional alteration may result from differences in the sites of action of neuropeptides.
evidence: Inferred from projection pattern differences

claim: The male-biased pPMp Gal neurons project extensively to various areas of the brain, especially to the dorsocaudal part of the telencephalon, thalamus, midbrain, cerebellum, and medulla oblongata.
source: We found that, in medaka, the male-biased pPMp Gal neurons project extensively to various areas of the brain, especially to the dorsocaudal part of the telencephalon, thalamus, midbrain, cerebellum, and medulla oblongata, suggesting that these areas are the primary sites of action of the Gal that is produced male-predominantly.
evidence: Shown by immunohistochemistry

claim: The dorsocaudal part of the telencephalon, thalamus, midbrain, cerebellum, and medulla oblongata are the primary sites of action of the Gal that is produced male-predominantly in medaka.
source: We found that, in medaka, the male-biased pPMp Gal neurons project extensively to various areas of the brain, especially to the dorsocaudal part of the telencephalon, thalamus, midbrain, cerebellum, and medulla oblongata, suggesting that these areas are the primary sites of action of the Gal that is produced male-predominantly.
evidence: Inferred from projection patterns and receptor distribution

claim: MPOA GAL neurons in mice intensely project to the anteroventral periventricular nucleus, paraventricular nucleus, dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and supraoptic nucleus.
source: Interestingly, however, their primary projection targets seem to be rather different from those in medaka: these neurons in mice intensely project to, for example, the anteroventral periventricular nucleus, paraventricular nucleus, dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and supraoptic nucleus (Kohl et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from mouse studies

claim: The projection targets of MPOA GAL neurons have diversified during evolution to facilitate species variation in the functional role of GAL.
source: This species difference suggests that the projection targets of MPOA GAL neurons have diversified during evolution to such an extent as to facilitate species variation in the functional role of GAL.
evidence: Inferred from comparative projection analysis

claim: In medaka, pPMp Gal neurons project densely to Dm and Dl in the dorsocaudal part of the telencephalon, where Galr1 is most widely and abundantly expressed.
source: We found that, in medaka, pPMp Gal neurons project densely to Dm and Dl in the dorsocaudal part of the telencephalon, where Galr1 is most widely and abundantly expressed.
evidence: Shown by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization

claim: Dm and Dl are considered homologous to the mammalian basolateral amygdala and hippocampus, respectively.
source: Dm and Dl are considered homologous to the mammalian basolateral amygdala and hippocampus, respectively, which lack direct projections from MPOA GAL neurons (O'Connell and Hofmann, 2011; Kohl et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from comparative neuroanatomy literature

claim: The mammalian basolateral amygdala and hippocampus lack direct projections from MPOA GAL neurons.
source: Dm and Dl are considered homologous to the mammalian basolateral amygdala and hippocampus, respectively, which lack direct projections from MPOA GAL neurons (O'Connell and Hofmann, 2011; Kohl et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from mouse studies

claim: Dm and Dl affect the decision to engage in social behaviors, including aggression, in both teleosts and mammals.
source: There is persuasive evidence both in teleosts and in mammals that these brain regions affect the decision to engage in social behaviors, including aggression (Demski, 2013; Leroy et al., 2018; Diaz and Lin, 2020).
evidence: Cited from behavioral neuroscience literature

claim: Gal produced in pPMp may exert its effects on chases primarily by influencing the activity of Dm and Dl.
source: Given this, Gal produced in pPMp may exert its effects on chases primarily by influencing the activity of these brain regions.
evidence: Inferred from projection patterns and known functions of target regions

claim: Overexpression of cAMP-responsive element-binding protein in the basolateral amygdala enhances the acquisition of conditioned defeat in Syrian hamsters.
source: In Syrian hamsters, overexpression of cAMP-responsive element-binding protein in the basolateral amygdala enhances the acquisition of conditioned defeat (Jasnow et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from hamster studies

claim: Neural activity in Dm and Dl is negatively correlated with the frequency of aggressive territorial defense in African cichlids.
source: In African cichlids (Astatotilapia burtoni), neural activity in Dm and Dl is negatively correlated with the frequency of aggressive territorial defense (Weitekamp and Hofmann, 2017; Weitekamp et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from cichlid studies

claim: Gal may promote chases by reducing the activity of Dm and Dl to block the acquisition of conditioned defeat via the inhibitory receptor Galr1.
source: Based on those observations, it is possible that Gal promotes chases by reducing the activity of these brain regions to block the acquisition of conditioned defeat via the inhibitory receptor Galr1, which robustly suppresses the cAMP pathway.
evidence: Speculated based on integration of multiple lines of evidence

claim: Chases are unique among aggressive acts in being initiated specifically by dominant males toward their subordinates after dominance relationships are established in zebrafish.
source: Studies in zebrafish (Danio rerio) have shown that chases are unique among aggressive acts in being initiated specifically by dominant males toward their subordinates after dominance relationships are established (Oliveira et al., 2011; Zabegalov et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from zebrafish studies

claim: Male medaka perform chases immediately after the first encounter and mutually rather than unilaterally.
source: Here, however, we observed that male medaka perform chases immediately after the first encounter (and thus before dominance relationships are established) and mutually rather than unilaterally; therefore, this possibility seems unlikely.
evidence: Observed from behavioral tests

claim: Gal may facilitate territoriality rather than aggression per se.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that Gal may facilitate territoriality rather than aggression per se.
evidence: Proposed as an alternative hypothesis

claim: Males of the territorial morph exhibit higher levels of brain gal expression as compared with non-territorial males in African cichlids, sunfish, and midshipman fish.
source: This latter view is supported by the observation in African cichlids, sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus), and midshipman fish that males of the territorial morph exhibit higher levels of brain gal expression as compared with non-territorial males (Renn et al., 2008; Partridge et al., 2016; Tripp et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from comparative teleost studies

claim: Experimental manipulations that alter the sex steroid milieu can lead to the reversal of sex-typical mating behaviors even in adulthood in teleosts, including medaka.
source: In teleosts, including medaka, experimental manipulations that alter the sex steroid milieu can lead to the reversal of sex-typical mating behaviors even in adulthood (Okubo et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from teleost behavioral studies

claim: Treating adult female medaka with androgen readily induced male-typical aggressive behaviors.
source: That observation has been further extended by the present finding that treating adult female medaka with androgen readily induced male-typical aggressive behaviors.
evidence: Demonstrated by androgen treatment experiments

claim: Brain and behavior of teleosts are highly sexually labile throughout their lifetime.
source: Hence, brain and behavior of teleosts are highly sexually labile throughout their lifetime.
evidence: Concluded from hormone manipulation experiments

claim: The pPMp population of Gal neurons may be a critical element of the neural mechanism underlying the labile nature of teleost brain and behavior.
source: Because of its behavioral role and reversible sexual dimorphism in response to sex steroids, the pPMp population of Gal neurons may be a critical element of the long-sought neural mechanism underlying the labile nature of teleost brain and behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the androgen-dependent and reversible nature of these neurons

claim: A subset of GAL neurons within the MPOA serve very different, even opposite, behavioral roles across species, probably due to their varying functional connections with the rest of the brain.
source: In summary, we have demonstrated that a subset of GAL neurons within the MPOA, the most highly conserved node of the social behavior network, serve very different, even opposite, behavioral roles across species, probably due to their varying functional connections with the rest of the brain.
evidence: Concluded from comparative analysis of medaka and mice

claim: The species variation in neuronal functioning has arisen under different evolutionary selective pressures in distinct species.
source: Presumably, the species variation in neuronal functioning has arisen under different evolutionary selective pressures in distinct species.
evidence: General evolutionary reasoning

claim: Males and females of the same species often experience different evolutionary pressures and consequently display distinct behavioral patterns.
source: Because males and females of the same species also often experience different evolutionary pressures and consequently display distinct behavioral patterns, sex differences can also occur in behaviorally relevant neurons.
evidence: General evolutionary and behavioral biology knowledge

claim: Sex differences have occurred in MPOA Gal neurons in teleosts.
source: Our findings indicate that this has indeed happened to MPOA Gal neurons in teleosts.
evidence: Demonstrated by the sexual dimorphism observed in this study
